usage: The noodles are nice and chewy
식감 = mouthfeel, used constantly in food reviews
doubled form = even chewier, very common
examples: This place's noodles are really chewy.
It's freshly pulled noodles, so it's super chewy.
The octopus isn't tough, it's pleasantly chewy, so I like it.
쫄깃하다 = good chewy, 질기다 = bad tough
nuance: 쫄깃하다 is the GOOD kind of chewy: bouncy and springy like fresh noodles, tteok, or well-cooked octopus. Koreans treat it as high praise for 식감 (texture), so saying 면이 쫄깃해요 at a restaurant is a real compliment. Do not confuse it with 질기다, which is the bad 'tough/rubbery' chewy.
mistakes: Using 쫄깃하다 for tough meat you can't bite through — that negative sense is 질기다, not 쫄깃하다.
Saying 쫄깃하는 — it's an adjective, so the present modifier is 쫄깃한 (쫄깃한 면), never 쫄깃하는.

usage: famous slang: 겉은 바삭 속은 촉촉
examples: Fried chicken has to be crispy to be good, as expected.
The fritters just came out, so they're super crispy.
여기 돈까스는 겉이 바삭하고 안은 부드러워요.
The pork cutlet here is crispy outside and soft inside.
nuance: 바삭하다 is the light, crisp crunch of fried chicken, twigim, fresh toast, or crackers. It is the key selling point of fried food in Korea, hence the famous phrase 겉바속촉 (crispy outside, moist inside). If something has lost its crisp and gone soggy, the word you want is the opposite, 눅눅하다.
mistakes: Mixing it up with 딱딱하다 (hard/stiff) — 바삭하다 is a light airy crunch, not rock-hard.
Using it for soggy leftover fries — once crispness is gone, Koreans say 눅눅해졌어요, not 바삭해요.

usage: set phrase for tangmuk, lemon candy, etc.
examples: The cold-noodle broth is tangy, so it whets my appetite.
These tangerines are really sweet-and-sour and delicious.
Spicy mixed noodles taste best when mixed tangy.
nuance: 새콤하다 is the appetizing, refreshing sour of vinegar, citrus, or 무침 dishes — it makes your mouth water rather than pucker. Compare it with plain 시다 (just 'sour') and 시큼하다 (a sharper, sometimes off sour). The combo 새콤달콤하다 (sweet-and-sour) is everywhere in food talk and ads.
mistakes: Using 새콤하다 for spoiled/off sourness — that unpleasant sour is closer to 시큼하다 or 쉬다(상하다).
Treating it as a verb: it's 새콤한 맛 / 새콤해요, never 새콤하는.

english: pleasantly spicy, with a nice kick
examples: Tteokbokki tastes best sweet-and-spicy, that's the real flavor.
The broth has a nice kick, so it settles my stomach.
안 맵게 말고 살짝 매콤하게 해 주세요.
Not no-spice, just make it a little bit spicy, please.
nuance: 매콤하다 is a pleasant, appetizing spiciness with a kick — softer and more positive than 맵다, which can mean painfully hot. Koreans use 매콤하다 to praise tteokbokki, jjigae, and dakgalbi, often as 매콤달콤하다 (sweet-and-spicy). When you order, 매콤하게 means 'give it a nice kick,' while 맵게 risks getting it fiery.
mistakes: Saying 너무 매콤해서 못 먹겠어요 for unbearably hot food — at that level Koreans switch to 매워서 못 먹겠어요.
Writing 매콤하는 — adjective forms are 매콤한 / 매콤해요, never 매콤하는.

usage: warm and spicy in the stomach
examples: On cold days, a hot spicy broth is the best.
How about a hearty spicy jjamppong to cure the hangover?
The broth is so hot-and-hearty I'm sweating.
nuance: 얼큰하다 describes the warming, full-bodied spicy heat of red broths like 김치찌개, 짬뽕, and 해장국 — it implies comfort and warmth, not just heat. It pairs almost exclusively with 국물 (broth/soup) and is a go-to word for cold days and hangover cures. (Note: 얼큰하다 can also slangily mean pleasantly tipsy, but the food sense is the everyday one.)
mistakes: Applying it to dry foods — 얼큰하다 is for broths/soups, so 얼큰한 치킨 sounds wrong.
Confusing it with 느끼하다 — they are unrelated; 얼큰하다 is hot-spicy, 느끼하다 is greasy.

usage: savory enough to go with rice
밥반찬 = side to eat with rice
examples: This soy-braised beef is so savory it's a 'rice thief.'
밥 도둑 = makes you eat lots of rice
Fries taste best when they're a little salty.
국이 짜지 않고 딱 짭짤하게 잘됐네요.
The soup isn't over-salty, it came out perfectly savory.
짜다 = too salty, 짭짤하다 = just-right salty
nuance: 짭짤하다 is the pleasant, savory saltiness that makes food moreish — think soy-braised dishes, fries, or dried squid. It is positive, unlike 짜다, which usually means unpleasantly over-salted. (Casual bonus: 짭짤하다 also means a side income is 'tidy/decent,' as in 부수입이 짭짤하다.)
mistakes: Using 짭짤하다 to complain food is too salty — for over-salted, say 짜요 instead.
Forgetting it's an adjective: 짭짤한 반찬 / 짭짤해요, not 짭짤하는.

usage: 비린내 = the fishy smell, very common
examples: 이 회 좀 비린 것 같아요.
This sashimi seems a bit fishy.
Squeezing lemon reduces the fishy smell.
It's so fresh it's not fishy at all.
nuance: 비리다 is almost always negative: the off, fishy taste or smell of seafood (or even blood) that isn't fresh. The noun 비린내 (fishy smell) is used just as much as the adjective. Saying 안 비려요 ('not fishy') is high praise for raw fish — freshness is judged largely by the absence of 비린 맛.
mistakes: The modifier is 비린, not 비리는 — it's an adjective, so 비린 맛 / 비린내, never the verb-style 비리는 맛.
Using 비리다 for general bad smells — it specifically means fishy/raw-seafood; for spoiled-rotten use 상한 냄새.

examples: 이 감 아직 안 익어서 떫어요.
This persimmon isn't ripe yet, so it's astringent.
Under-steeped tea is a bit astringent.
This wine has a strong tannic taste.
nuance: 떫다 is that dry, mouth-puckering astringency of unripe persimmons, strong tea, or tannic wine — the sensation that makes your tongue feel rough. It is a distinct taste category in Korean alongside sweet/salty/sour/bitter/spicy, and persimmons (감) are the classic reference point. The conjugation is regular: 떫어요, 떫은, 떫고.
mistakes: Confusing 떫다 (astringent) with 쓰다 (bitter) — coffee is 쓰다, an unripe persimmon is 떫다.
Treating it as a verb: it's an adjective, so 떫은 감 / 떫어요, never 떫는 감 or 떫는다.

examples: This broth isn't greasy, it's clean-tasting.
목 넘김 = the way it goes down the throat
The gukbap here is clean-tasting, so I come often.
nuance: Beyond meaning 'tidy/neat,' 깔끔하다 is a big food-review word for a clean, crisp, non-greasy flavor — the opposite of 느끼하다 (greasy/cloying). It's used to praise clear broths, light beer, or anything that finishes without a heavy aftertaste. You'll hear 깔끔해요 constantly in mukbang and restaurant reviews.
mistakes: Assuming 깔끔하다 only means 'tidy' — in food contexts it specifically praises a clean, non-greasy taste.
Pairing it with rich greasy dishes — calling fatty pork belly 깔끔하다 is contradictory; that's 느끼하다.

usage: also used for smells, not just taste
examples: This cake is sweet just right and delicious.
The strawberries are sweet-and-sour, so I keep eating them.
It's not too sweet, just subtly sweet.
nuance: 달콤하다 is a pleasant, appealing sweetness, often subtler or more romantic-sounding than plain 달다 (which can imply 'too sweet'). It works for desserts, fruit, and even aromas, and shows up constantly in the combos 새콤달콤 (sweet-sour) and 달콤짭짤 (sweet-salty). Figuratively it also means 'sweet/blissful,' as in 달콤한 휴식.
mistakes: Saying 달콤해서 못 먹겠어요 for sickly-sweet food — for 'too sweet to eat,' use 너무 달아서 못 먹겠어요.
Adjective forms only: 달콤한 / 달콤해요, never 달콤하는.

examples: 우유에서 시큼한 냄새가 나요. 상한 것 같아요.
The milk smells sour. I think it's gone bad.
It's aged kimchi, so it's a bit sharply sour.
이 빵 시큼한 거 보니 사워도우인가 봐요.
This bread tastes sour, so it must be sourdough.
nuance: 시큼하다 is a sharper, more piercing sour than the appetizing 새콤하다 — it can describe well-fermented kimchi or sourdough, but also food that has started to spoil. Context decides whether it's positive (묵은지, sourdough) or a warning sign (sour milk). When in doubt about freshness, 시큼한 냄새 is the phrase that flags 'this might be off.'
mistakes: Using 시큼하다 when you mean the pleasant tangy sour of citrus or dressing — that's 새콤하다.
It's an adjective: 시큼한 / 시큼해요, not 시큼하는.

english: tough, chewy in a bad way (hard to chew)
examples: 이 고기 너무 질겨서 못 먹겠어요.
This meat is so tough I can't eat it.
I cooked it long and it actually got tougher.
If the squid is fresh, it's not tough.
nuance: 질기다 is the BAD chewy: meat or seafood so tough and rubbery it's hard to bite through — the exact opposite of the praised 쫄깃하다 (pleasantly springy). Learners constantly mix these two up, so anchor it: tough overcooked steak is 질겨요, fresh bouncy noodles are 쫄깃해요. It can also describe a stubborn, persistent personality (질긴 인연).
mistakes: Swapping 질기다 and 쫄깃하다 — 질기다 is the negative 'tough/rubbery,' 쫄깃하다 is the positive 'springy.'
Treating it as a verb: 질긴 고기 / 질겨요, not 질기는.
